clinicalPearls: The most common cause of neonatal cholestasis leading to liver transplantation, resulting from progressive inflammatory obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts.
Classic presentation is a term infant with prolonged jaundice, pale (acholic) stools, and dark urine, usually with otherwise good early growth.
Any infant jaundiced beyond about two weeks of age should have a fractionated bilirubin measured; a raised conjugated (direct) fraction signals cholestasis and needs urgent evaluation.
Early diagnosis is critical because the success of surgery falls sharply with age, ideally before about 8 weeks (60 days) of life.
The Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy aims to restore bile drainage; the earlier it is performed, the better the chance of clearing jaundice.
Even after a successful Kasai procedure, many children progress to cirrhosis and ultimately require liver transplantation.
A subset have the biliary atresia splenic malformation syndrome with situs and other congenital anomalies.
Ultrasound may show an absent or small gallbladder and the 'triangular cord' sign; a hepatobiliary scan shows hepatic uptake without excretion into the bowel.
reference.pathophysiology: A fibro-obliterative process destroys the extrahepatic and often intrahepatic bile ducts, obstructing bile flow. Retained bile causes progressive hepatocellular injury, portal tract inflammation, and bile ductular proliferation, leading to fibrosis and, if untreated, biliary cirrhosis with portal hypertension and liver failure. The initiating cause is uncertain and probably heterogeneous, involving developmental, immune, and possibly viral mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: Alagille syndrome and other intrahepatic cholestatic syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Liver function tests including GGT and aminotransferases
Abdominal ultrasound (gallbladder, triangular cord sign, exclusion of choledochal cyst)
Hepatobiliary scintigraphy assessing excretion into the intestine
Intraoperative cholangiogram to confirm the diagnosis
Studies to exclude alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency and metabolic causes
redFlags: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia at any age in an infant
Jaundice persisting beyond two weeks of life
Signs of coagulopathy or vitamin K deficiency bleeding
Hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, or other features of advanced liver disease
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on the age at surgery; early Kasai portoenterostomy can restore bile flow and delay or avoid transplantation, but many children eventually progress to end-stage liver disease. Overall long-term survival is good when transplantation is available.
pitfalls: Dismissing prolonged neonatal jaundice as physiological or breast-milk jaundice without checking a split bilirubin
Delaying referral and surgery beyond the window where the Kasai procedure is most effective
Relying on a normal ultrasound to exclude the diagnosis
Overlooking associated congenital anomalies in the splenic malformation syndrome
management: Early Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy to restore bile drainage, performed as soon as possible while the infant is young, since success falls sharply with age
Post-Kasai ursodeoxycholic acid to promote bile flow and prophylactic antibiotics against ascending cholangitis
Aggressive nutritional support with high-energy medium-chain-triglyceride feeds and supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K
Prompt recognition and antibiotic treatment of cholangitis episodes
Surveillance and management of evolving biliary cirrhosis and portal hypertension, including varices, ascites and growth
Liver transplantation for a failed Kasai procedure or progression to end-stage liver disease
Paediatric hepatology and transplant multidisciplinary care with family support and counselling
